explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Verse 4 says, “Those who had been scattered preached the word wherever they went.” Think about that. They got shoved out of their homes, and the first thing they did was start talking about Jesus. Where I got scattered, all I did was gather dust.

I get why you'd pick it. Getting scattered feels like a reason to lie low. But Acts 8:4 says, “…preached the word wherever they went.” Nobody in that verse is behind a curtain whispering. They're out in the open, talking.

Nope, friend, they were scattered away from there. The verse says they preached the word wherever they went, so wherever they landed, that's where the preaching happened. Peter and John are the ones who head back to Jerusalem later in this passage (Acts 8:25). These believers were busy right where they stood.

Right on the money. Verse 5 says Philip, one of the scattered believers, “proclaimed the Christ to them.” He went down to a city in Samaria with one message, and it was about Jesus. No side topics, no warm-up act.
Close to the neighborhood, but no. Acts 8:5 says Philip, one of the scattered believers, proclaimed the Christ to them. The whole message centered on Him. The word prophets isn't in that verse.

Good guess for a Bible word, but it's not in this verse. Philip, one of the scattered believers, “proclaimed the Christ” in that Samaritan city (Acts 8:5). His message was about a Person, and the Sabbath never comes up. I once tried to build a whole batch around a recipe that wasn't on the card, and it did NOT go well.

explanations.answer: The signs they see him perform
explanations.explanation: Yes! Verse 6 says the crowds paid close attention “to Philip’s message and to the signs they saw him perform.” They heard it and they saw it. That's a crowd with its eyes AND its ears wide open.

Nice try, baker, but no scrolls show up in this verse. Acts 8:6 says the crowds paid attention to the signs they saw him perform. They were watching something happen, not listening to a reading. Nobody there was squinting at fine print.

Love the energy, but there's no choir in this verse. The crowds paid close attention to Philip's message and to the signs they saw him perform (Acts 8:6). Singing lessons aren't mentioned. I'd have signed up, though. My voice needs all the help it can get.

That's not what the text says. Acts 8:7 says, “With loud shrieks, unclean spirits came out of many who were possessed…” Loud shrieks, baker. Nobody tiptoed out the back door and left a thank-you note.

Correct, it's False. The verse says, “With loud shrieks, unclean spirits came out of many who were possessed…” (Acts 8:7). Those spirits did NOT leave quietly. Whatever happened in that city, you could hear it.
Yes, joy! Verse 8 says, “So there was great joy in that city.” Spirits came out and the paralyzed and lame were healed. I think that city had the best day it had ever had.
I see why you'd think it, after the loud shrieks. But the verse lands somewhere else. Acts 8:8 says, “So there was great joy in that city.” The word fear isn't there.
Not mourning, friend. After the spirits left and the paralyzed and lame were healed, Acts 8:8 says, “So there was great joy in that city.” People who couldn't walk were walking. That's a day for joy.

You got it. Acts 8:9 says Simon “had practiced sorcery in the city and astounded the people of Samaria.” He had that city's attention before Philip ever walked in. Remember that, because it matters later in the story.
I can see the thinking, since Simon had people's attention. But Acts 8:9 says he “had practiced sorcery in the city.” Nothing about medicine there. He astounded the people with sorcery.
Close in sound, but no. Acts 8:9 says Simon, who was already in that city when Philip came, “had practiced sorcery.” Prophecy isn't the word the verse uses. The Bible calls it sorcery, and so do I.
That's the one. The people said, “This man is the divine power called the Great Power” (Acts 8:10). From the least to the greatest, they all heeded his words. That's a big name to hang on one man.

That's a great title, but it isn't the one in this passage. In Acts 8:10 the people say, “This man is the divine power called the Great Power.” That's what they called Simon. Nobody in Samaria was handing out hunting titles.
That sounds like a reasonable title, but it's not what they said. Acts 8:10 has the people saying, “This man is the divine power called the Great Power.” That's the name they gave Simon.

Not quite, baker. Verse 11 says people paid close attention to Simon “…he had astounded them for a long time with his sorcery.” A long time. He wasn't some newcomer with a flyer. He'd been the main attraction for a while.

Right, it's False. Acts 8:11 says the people paid close attention to him because “…he had astounded them for a long time with his sorcery.” That's years of habit, not a brand new fan club. Simon had been the talk of the city long before Philip showed up.

That's the word. Acts 8:12 says, “…they were baptized, both men and women.” They believed Philip as he preached the gospel of the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ. Belief came first, then baptism.

I see where that came from, since scattering started this whole story. But in Acts 8:12, the people who believed Philip were baptized, both men and women. Scattered describes what happened to the believers from Jerusalem back in verse 4. Here it's baptism.
Good church word, but it's not in this verse. Acts 8:12 says that when they believed Philip, “…they were baptized, both men and women.” That's what happened next. Nobody got handed a title.

Yes. Verse 13 says Simon “followed Philip closely and was astounded by the great signs and miracles he observed.” This is the same Simon who astounded people for years. Now the shoe is on the other foot, and I bet it felt strange.
Crowds are in the story, but they're not what astounded Simon. Acts 8:13 says he “was astounded by the great signs and miracles he observed.” He was watching what Philip did, not counting heads.
Nice guess, but the law doesn't come up here. Acts 8:13 says Simon followed Philip closely and was astounded by the great signs and miracles he observed. What he watched were signs and miracles.
Yes, Peter, one of the apostles. Verse 14 says the apostles in Jerusalem “sent Peter and John to them.” He goes up in the story with a partner.
Right, John goes with Peter. Acts 8:14 says the apostles in Jerusalem sent Peter and John to Samaria. These two make the trip together, so one of them always has company.
James, one of the twelve apostles (Matthew 10:2), is a fine name, but he isn't in this verse. Acts 8:14 says the apostles sent Peter and John. Keep him in your pocket for another passage.
Andrew, Peter's brother (Matthew 10:2), didn't make this trip in the verse. Acts 8:14 says the apostles sent Peter and John. So Andrew stays off this particular guest list.
Thomas, one of the twelve apostles (Matthew 10:3), isn't named here. In Acts 8:14 the apostles send Peter and John to Samaria. Those are the two names the verse gives us.
That's the prayer. Acts 8:15 says Peter and John prayed “for them to receive the Holy Spirit.” That was their first move when they got there.
Good prayer, but it's not the one in the verse. Acts 8:15 says Peter and John “prayed for them to receive the Holy Spirit.” Courage isn't mentioned. The prayer is about the Spirit.

I get why Saul would be on your mind. He's the man dragging believers off to prison (Acts 8:3). But Acts 8:15 says Peter and John prayed for the believers to receive the Holy Spirit. Saul doesn't come up in that prayer.
Not so, baker. Acts 8:16 says, “For the Holy Spirit had not yet fallen upon any of them…” Not any of them. They had been baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus, and the Spirit hadn't fallen yet.

That's right, it's False. The text says, “For the Holy Spirit had not yet fallen upon any of them; they had simply been baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus” (Acts 8:16). Not many, not some, none yet. Then Peter and John laid their hands on them, and they received the Holy Spirit (Acts 8:17).

Yep, money. Acts 8:18 says that when Simon saw the Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles' hands, “he offered them money.” He walks up with his wallet out. I think that's the moment the room got awkward.
Interesting idea, but the verse says something else. Acts 8:18 says Simon “offered them money.” His followers aren't part of the offer.
That would be a big offer, but it's not in the text. Acts 8:18 says Simon saw the Spirit given through the laying on of hands, and “he offered them money.” That's all he put on the table.

explanations.answer: The power to give the Holy Spirit
explanations.explanation: That's what he asked for. Simon said, “Give me this power as well… so that everyone on whom I lay my hands may receive the Holy Spirit” (Acts 8:19). He wanted to be the one handing it out. Peter's answer comes next.

That's not what Simon asks for here. In Acts 8:19 he says, “Give me this power as well,” so that everyone on whom he lays his hands may receive the Holy Spirit. The request is about power, not forgiveness.

Reasonable guess, but the text doesn't say that. Simon's words in Acts 8:19 are, “Give me this power as well,” so that everyone he lays hands on may receive the Holy Spirit. That's the power he's asking for.
Yes, gift. Peter says, “May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could buy the gift of God with money!” (Acts 8:20). A gift can't be bought, baker. That's the whole point of a gift.
The word of God is all over Acts, but not in this line. Peter says Simon thought he could “buy the gift of God with money” (Acts 8:20). The word that fits is gift.
House is a fun guess, but Peter didn't say it. In Acts 8:20 he says Simon “thought you could buy the gift of God with money.” Gift is the word that fits.

explanations.answer: His heart is not right before God
explanations.explanation: That's the reason Peter gives. He tells Simon, “You have no part or share in our ministry, because your heart is not right before God” (Acts 8:21). It's about his heart. I think that's a hard thing to hear.
The text never says that. Peter's reason in Acts 8:21 is, “…your heart is not right before God.” Simon followed Philip closely, according to verse 13. The problem Peter names is the heart.
That's not the reason Peter gives. In Acts 8:21 he says, “…your heart is not right before God.” Sorcery isn't what he points to there. The reason is the heart.
That's the word. Peter says, “Perhaps He will forgive you for the intent of your heart” (Acts 8:22). He had just told Simon to repent and pray to the Lord. The door is still open.

That might fit your mood after the rebuke, but it's not what Peter says. Acts 8:22 says, “Perhaps He will forgive you for the intent of your heart.” After telling Simon to repent and pray, the next word is forgive.
Not reward, friend. Peter says, “Perhaps He will forgive you for the intent of your heart” (Acts 8:22). Forgiveness is what he points Simon toward, and that's the word the verse uses.
Correct, it's True. Simon answers, “Pray to the Lord for me, so that nothing you have said may happen to me” (Acts 8:24). He's asking Peter and John to pray for him. I think he's rattled.

It's actually True. Acts 8:24 says Simon answered, “Pray to the Lord for me, so that nothing you have said may happen to me.” So he does ask for prayer. He asks Peter and John to pray, so he isn't brushing off what he heard.
Yes, they preach. Acts 8:25 says they returned to Jerusalem, “preaching the gospel in many of the Samaritan villages.” They were not coasting home. The trip back turned into a preaching tour.

I can see why offerings come to mind after Simon's money. But Acts 8:25 says Peter and John returned to Jerusalem, “preaching the gospel in many of the Samaritan villages.” Offerings aren't mentioned. They were preaching.

Nice guess, but that's not in this verse. Acts 8:25 says Peter and John were “preaching the gospel in many of the Samaritan villages” on their way back to Jerusalem. The text gives no elders. It gives preaching.
